summary: An Earth observation workspace built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Explore a satellite map, select a region, and inspect changes over time using Sentinel-1 C-band radar or NISAR L-band radar.
details:
AERO-WATCH: watching Earth’s surface dance through the clouds

What it does and how it works
AERO-WATCH is an open-source, browser-based workspace that turns NISAR radar data into interactive maps of surface change. A user searches for a place, draws a rectangle on the map (or picks a ready-made location), chooses a date range, and watches the changes play out over time.

The app has two NISAR analysis modes:

  • Flood tracking. It maps new open water on each acquisition date compared with the first, and estimates how long each area stayed flooded. Ready-made reference locations include the Limpopo River (Mozambique), Jamuna (Bangladesh), Indus (Pakistan), Mekong (Cambodia) and Mississippi (USA).
  • Vegetation and deforestation tracking. It estimates vegetation cover on each date from the HV polarization, and reports loss or gain between dates. Saved examples cover the Amazon, the Congo Basin and Borneo.

A Sentinel-1 C-band forest mode adds a monthly record for 2025, before NISAR’s July 2025 launch.

Behind the interface, a Python server searches NASA Earthdata for NISAR L2 GCOV products. It keeps only images from the same orbit track, direction, frame and mode, so every date lines up on the same pixel grid. It streams only the part of each multi-gigabyte HDF5 file that covers the selected area. It averages 4×4 pixels in linear power to reduce radar speckle (10 m to 40 m), converts the values to decibels, and then runs the analysis.

For floods, a pixel counts as open water when it is dark in both polarizations (HH < −15 dB and HV < −24 dB). Thresholds were chosen from the valley between the water and land peaks of the histogram. The ocean is masked with a land layer, permanent water and baseline water are excluded, and small noisy patches are removed. Results appear as map overlays on a timeline that users can scrub, play, or compare with the baseline. They can be downloaded as CSV and GeoTIFF files.

Benefits

  • Radar works day and night and through clouds, so floods can be seen during the storms that cause them, when optical satellites are blind.
  • Users need no radar expertise, no software installation and no downloads of multi-gigabyte files.
  • Outputs are standard GIS files, so analysts can reuse them directly.
  • The same pipeline works anywhere NISAR has data, simply by drawing a new region.

Intended impact
We want to make NISAR’s new L-band data accessible to people who make decisions on the ground: disaster responders, local authorities, resource managers, educators and the public. Seeing where water spreads, and for how long, helps prioritize response and understand flood patterns. Seeing vegetation change helps monitor forests. Because the project is open source, others can adapt it to new regions and new types of surface change.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python (backend and processing) and JavaScript, HTML and CSS (frontend).
  • Data processing: earthaccess (NASA Earthdata), h5py, NumPy, SciPy, pyproj, rasterio, Shapely, Cartopy / Natural Earth, Pillow.
  • Frontend: Leaflet with Esri, CARTO, OpenStreetMap and NASA GIBS basemaps, and OpenStreetMap Nominatim for location search. No build tools are required.
  • Data: NASA–ISRO NISAR L2 GCOV (L-band, HH/HV), and Sentinel-1 through Google Earth Engine.
  • Development: Jupyter / Google Colab for prototyping the method, and Git/GitHub. The project runs on an ordinary laptop with no special hardware.

Creativity

  • Users don’t just view static images: they watch Earth’s “dance” through animated timelines and a one-click baseline comparison.
  • The app streams only the needed part of huge radar files, which makes interactive analysis practical in a browser.
  • Display-only image enhancements and simple color views make radar images easier for non-experts to read.
  • One interface covers two kinds of change (water and vegetation) and two radar frequencies (L-band and C-band).

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific honesty. Results are labeled as estimates, not validated products. Flood mapping shows new open water relative to the first date and doesn’t detect water under vegetation. The thresholds need regional calibration, and our sensitivity tests showed the detected area can vary a lot with them, so we present ranges.
  • Data consistency. Mixing different orbits or frames creates false change, so the pipeline enforces one consistent stack.
  • Performance. Files are several gigabytes, so we used region-only streaming, caching, multilooking, and job timeouts.
  • Usability. We kept the workflow simple (draw, choose dates, analyze), with keyboard shortcuts and saved examples that work without any login.
  • Reproducibility. The code is open, with tests, CSV/GeoTIFF exports and documented methods.
